sections.heading: Overview
body: Railway Recruitment Board - Junior / Senior Section Engineer

sections.heading: About the Examination
body: The Railway Recruitment Board (RRB) Junior Engineer (JE) and Senior Section Engineer (SSE) examinations are highly sought-after national-level recruitment drives conducted to select technical supervisors for the Indian Railways. These roles form the backbone of the railway's technical workforce, ensuring the safe and efficient operation of one of the world's largest rail networks.

Note: While JE recruitment is conducted periodically based on vacancies, the direct recruitment for the SSE post has been paused in recent years, with these positions being filled through internal promotions. This guide covers the process generally applicable to both, with a focus on the current JE recruitment pattern.

sections.heading: The Philosophy Behind the Examination
body: Unlike administrative exams, the RRB JE/SSE selection process is engineered to identify candidates with strong technical foundations, problem-solving skills, and a steadfast commitment to safety and precision . The examination seeks to evaluate a candidate's:
Technical Proficiency: A deep and practical understanding of core engineering principles relevant to their specific discipline.
Analytical and Logical Reasoning: The ability to quickly analyze technical problems and arrive at logical solutions under pressure.
General Awareness & Scientific Temper: A solid understanding of basic science and an awareness of current affairs, crucial for a well-rounded technical supervisor.
Physical and Medical Fitness: The capacity to meet the stringent medical standards required for jobs that are critical to railway safety and operations.
The Posts and Departments

Successful candidates are allocated to various technical departments within the Indian Railways based on their engineering discipline, merit, and medical fitness. These roles are pivotal in the construction, maintenance, and operation of railway infrastructure.

sections.heading: The Multi-Stage Selection Process
body: The RRB JE selection is a rigorous multi-stage process designed to filter candidates based on technical knowledge, aptitude, and medical fitness.

Stage 1: First Stage Computer Based Test (CBT-1): This is a common screening test for all candidates, regardless of their engineering discipline. It is an objective-type (MCQ) exam designed to test general aptitude, reasoning, and scientific knowledge. Its primary purpose is to shortlist a large number of applicants for the next stage. Marks from this stage are not counted for the final merit list.

Stage 2: Second Stage Computer Based Test (CBT-2): This is the main technical examination and the real test of a candidate's domain knowledge. Candidates who clear CBT-1 are eligible for this stage. It consists of both common subjects and a large section dedicated to the specific technical discipline of the candidate. The score in this stage is the sole determinant of a candidate's position in the final merit list.

Stage 3: Document Verification (DV) and Medical Examination: Candidates shortlisted based on their CBT-2 performance are called for Document Verification. Here, all original academic and category certificates are verified. Following a successful DV, candidates are sent for a mandatory and stringent medical examination at a designated Railway Hospital. Clearing the medical test according to the standards prescribed for the post is non-negotiable.
The Final Verdict: Panel and Appointment

A final panel of selected candidates is prepared purely based on the marks obtained in the Second Stage CBT (CBT-2) , provided they clear the Document Verification and the required Medical Examination. Candidates are then allocated a zone and post, marking the beginning of their career as a Junior Engineer in the Indian Railways.

sections.heading: Typical Timeline (Indicative)
body: Unlike the fixed annual calendar of UPSC, RRB recruitments are not conducted every year. They are announced based on the vacancies reported by various railway zones. The entire process, from notification to the final panel, can take anywhere from 1 to 2 years.
Disclaimer: This is a generic timeline based on past recruitment drives. Always refer to the official Centralised Employment Notification (CEN) for exact dates.
Phase 1: Notification & Application (Month 1-2)

Notification Release: The official Centralised Employment Notification (CEN) is published in the Employment News and on all official RRB websites, detailing vacancies, eligibility, syllabus, and dates.
Application Period: The online application window opens and typically remains active for about 30 days .

sections.heading: Phase 2: First Stage CBT (Month 4-6)
body: Application Status & City Intimation: RRBs release the application status and inform candidates of their exam city and date about 10-15 days before the exam.
Admit Card Release: The e-Admit Card (Hall Ticket) can be downloaded 4 days prior to the candidate's specific exam date.
CBT-1 Examination: The exam is conducted online in multiple shifts over several days or weeks across the country.
Phase 3: CBT-1 Result & CBT-2 Shortlisting (Month 7-8)
Answer Key & Objections: A provisional answer key is released, and candidates are given a window to raise objections.

CBT-1 Result: The results, including the scores (raw and normalized) and the list of candidates shortlisted for CBT-2, are published. The number of candidates shortlisted is typically 15 times the number of vacancies.

sections.heading: Phase 4: Second Stage CBT (Month 9-10)
body: Admit Card for CBT-2: Similar to CBT-1, admit cards are released 4 days before the exam date.
CBT-2 Examination: The technical stage of the exam is conducted, also in multiple shifts.
Phase 5: CBT-2 Result & DV Shortlisting (Month 12-14)
Answer Key & Result: The answer key and final result for CBT-2 are declared.
DV Shortlisting: A list of candidates shortlisted for Document Verification is published, usually in a 1:1 ratio (or slightly more) to the number of vacancies.
Phase 6: Document Verification & Medical Exam (Month 15-18)
DV Schedule: Shortlisted candidates are called for DV at the respective RRB headquarters on specific dates.
Medical Examination: Immediately after DV, candidates are issued a memo and sent to the designated Railway Hospital for the medical examination, which may take 2-4 days.
Phase 7: Final Panel & Joining (Month 19 onwards)
Final Result (Panel): After compiling the results of DV and the medical exam, the RRB publishes the final panel of selected candidates.
Appointment: The respective Zonal Railways then handle the process of issuing appointment letters and conducting training.

sections.heading: Eligibility Criteria
body: Aspirants must ensure they meet all the eligibility criteria mentioned in the official notification regarding Nationality, Age, and Educational Qualifications. These criteria are strictly enforced.
Note: The details provided here are based on the latest recruitment patterns. The official CEN for the examination year is the final authority.
1. Nationality

sections.heading: A candidate must be
body: A citizen of India, or
A subject of Nepal, or
A subject of Bhutan, or
A Tibetan refugee who came over to India before January 1, 1962, with the intention of permanently settling in India, or
A person of Indian origin (PIO) who has migrated from Pakistan, Burma, Sri Lanka, East African countries, etc., with the intention of permanently settling in India.
2. Age Limit (for RRB JE)
The age is calculated as of a cut-off date mentioned in the notification (e.g., 1st January of the recruitment year).
Minimum Age: 18 years
Maximum Age: 33 years (for the General/UR category)
Relaxations in the upper age limit are provided for reserved categories:
3. Educational Qualification (as on closing date of application)
This is the most critical criterion. The required qualification must be from a recognized University/Institute.

For Junior Engineer (JE): A candidate must possess either: A three-year Diploma in the relevant engineering discipline specified for the post. A B.E. / B.Tech / B.Sc (Engineering) degree in the relevant engineering discipline.
A three-year Diploma in the relevant engineering discipline specified for the post.
A B.E. / B.Tech / B.Sc (Engineering) degree in the relevant engineering discipline.
For Depot Material Superintendent (DMS): A three-year Diploma or a Degree in Engineering from any discipline.
For Chemical & Metallurgical Assistant (CMA): Bachelor's Degree in Science with Physics and Chemistry with a minimum of 45% marks.

Important: Candidates who are awaiting the results of their final examinations are NOT eligible to apply. The educational qualification must be fully completed on or before the closing date of the application.

sections.heading: Stages, Exam Pattern & Marking Scheme
body: The RRB JE selection process is composed of two stages of Computer Based Tests (CBTs), followed by Document Verification and a mandatory Medical Examination.

sections.heading: Stage 1: First Stage CBT (Common Screening Test)
body: This is a qualifying test to screen candidates for the second stage. The marks from this stage are not used for the final merit list. The level of questions is generally of the 10th/12th standard.
Duration: 90 minutes (120 minutes for eligible PwBD candidates).
Negative Marking: Yes. 1/3rd of a mark is deducted for every incorrect answer.
Normalization: Marks are normalized across different shifts to account for variations in difficulty levels.
Minimum Qualifying Marks: UR-40%, OBC-30%, SC-30%, ST-25%.

sections.heading: Stage 2: Second Stage CBT (Technical & Merit-Deciding Stage)
body: This stage decides the final merit of the candidates. The exam is divided into two parts, conducted in a single session.
Duration: 120 minutes (160 minutes for eligible PwBD candidates).
Virtual Calculator: An on-screen scientific calculator will be provided for calculations. Physical calculators are not allowed.
Merit Calculation: The final panel is prepared solely based on the normalized marks obtained in this stage.

name: UPSC CAPF (AC)
summary: UPSC Central Armed Police Forces (Assistant Commandants) Examination

sections.heading: Overview
body: UPSC Central Armed Police Forces (Assistant Commandants) Examination

sections.heading: About the Examination
body: The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) Examination is a national-level competitive exam for the recruitment of Assistant Commandants (AC) , who are Group 'A' officers. This examination serves as the unified gateway for aspiring candidates to join the officer cadre of India's premier internal security forces. It is a highly respected career path that offers a unique blend of adventure, responsibility, and service to the nation.

sections.heading: The Philosophy Behind the Examination
body: The CAPF (AC) examination is designed to select young, dynamic, and resilient leaders. Beyond academic knowledge, the selection process rigorously assesses a candidate's physical and mental fortitude, integrity, and suitability for command roles in challenging operational environments. The exam seeks individuals who possess:
Physical and Mental Robustness: The ability to endure tough physical conditions and maintain composure under extreme pressure.
Leadership and Command Quality: The potential to lead a company of armed personnel, make critical decisions, and inspire confidence.
Intellectual Acuity: A strong grasp of general awareness, analytical reasoning, and security-related issues.
Unwavering Integrity: A strong moral compass and a deep sense of patriotism and duty.
The Forces at Stake

Successful candidates are appointed as Assistant Commandants in one of the five Central Armed Police Forces under the Ministry of Home Affairs. These forces are the pillars of India's internal security architecture.

sections.heading: The Three-Stage Selection Process
body: The CAPF (AC) selection is a multi-stage process designed to comprehensively evaluate a candidate's fitness for the role. The entire cycle spans over a year.

Stage 1: Written Examination: This is the first filter and consists of two papers conducted on the same day. Paper I is an objective test of General Ability and Intelligence, while Paper II is a descriptive test of General Studies, Essay, and Comprehension. This stage assesses the academic and analytical capabilities of the candidates.

Stage 2: Physical Standards Test (PST) / Physical Efficiency Test (PET) & Medical Standards Test: Candidates who qualify the written exam are called for this stage. The PST involves checking physical measurements like height and chest. The PET includes a series of athletic events to test physical endurance and agility. This is followed by a detailed medical examination to ensure candidates meet the stringent health requirements. This stage is qualifying in nature .

Stage 3: Interview / Personality Test: The final stage is an interview conducted by a board of senior officers and experts at the UPSC. This test assesses the candidate's personality, leadership potential, communication skills, and overall suitability for a command position in the armed police forces.
The Final Verdict: Merit and Allocation

The final merit list is prepared based on the total marks obtained in the Written Examination (450 marks) and the Interview/Personality Test (150 marks) , for a grand total of 600 marks. Based on their final rank and the preferences submitted by them, candidates are allocated to one of the five CAPFs.

sections.heading: Typical Timeline (Indicative)
body: The UPSC CAPF (AC) Examination follows a relatively predictable annual schedule. Understanding this timeline is essential for planning your preparation effectively.
Disclaimer: These timelines are based on past trends. Always refer to the official UPSC calendar for the specific year for exact dates.
Phase 1: Notification & Application (April - May)
Late April: The official notification for the CAPF (AC) Examination is released by UPSC on its website (upsc.gov.in).
April - May: The online application window opens and typically remains active for about 20-25 days.
Phase 2: Written Examination (August)
July: The e-Admit Card for the Written Examination is released approximately 3 weeks before the exam date.
First Sunday of August: The Written Examination (Paper I & Paper II) is conducted on a single day across the country.
Phase 3: Written Exam Result (September - October)
The results of the Written Examination are typically declared within 40-50 days. A list of qualified candidates is published, who must then fill a Detailed Application Form (DAF).
Phase 4: PST / PET & Medical Tests (December - February)
Qualified candidates are called for the Physical and Medical tests. These are conducted in batches at various centers designated by the Nodal Authority (like ITBP, BSF, etc.).
Phase 5: Interview / Personality Test (May - June of next year)

Unlike civilian services, the CDS exam is the primary gateway for university graduates to embark on a challenging and honourable career leading the men and women of the Indian Army, Navy, and Air Force.

body: The CDS selection process is designed to identify candidates who possess the unique blend of attributes required for military leadership, often summarized as "Officer Like Qualities" (OLQs). The exam assesses more than academic knowledge; it seeks individuals with:
Mental Robustness & Aptitude: The ability to think clearly, solve problems logically, and perform under pressure.
Physical Fitness & Courage: A high standard of physical and mental endurance to meet the demanding nature of military life.
Leadership & Integrity: The potential to lead, inspire confidence, and uphold the highest standards of honour and integrity.
Patriotism & Sense of Duty: A deep-seated commitment to the nation and an unwavering sense of duty and responsibility.

sections.heading: The Two-Stage Selection Process
body: The CDS selection is a comprehensive two-stage process designed to thoroughly evaluate a candidate's suitability for a commission in the Armed Forces.

Stage 1: Written Examination: This is an objective-type (MCQ) examination designed to test the candidate's knowledge of English, General Knowledge, and Elementary Mathematics. It serves as a screening test to select candidates for the next stage. Candidates applying only for the Officers' Training Academy (OTA) are exempted from the Mathematics paper.

Stage 2: Services Selection Board (SSB) Interview: Candidates who qualify in the written exam are called for the SSB Interview. This is an intensive 5-day personality and intelligence assessment. It includes a battery of psychological tests, group tasks, and a personal interview to evaluate a candidate's "Officer Like Qualities" (OLQs). This stage is the ultimate test of one's character, leadership potential, and mental fortitude.
The Final Verdict: Merit and Joining Instructions

A final merit list is prepared based on the total marks obtained in the Written Examination and the SSB Interview . Candidates who clear the medical examination are issued joining instructions for their respective academies based on their rank, preferences, and the number of vacancies available.

sections.heading: The Philosophy Behind the Examination
body: The CSE is engineered to assess more than just rote memorization. Its core philosophy is to identify individuals who possess a potent combination of intellectual depth, analytical acuity, ethical integrity, and a profound sense of social commitment . The examination seeks to evaluate a candidate's:
Critical Assimilation: The ability to understand complex information from diverse fields, filter out noise, and grasp the core issues.
Balance of Judgment: The capacity to form reasoned opinions, consider multiple perspectives, and make sound, unbiased judgments under pressure.
Intellectual and Moral Integrity: A strong ethical compass, honesty, and the courage to uphold constitutional values.
Leadership and Social Cohesion: The potential to lead, inspire, and work collaboratively to solve pressing societal problems.
Awareness and Curiosity: A deep and abiding interest in the world around them, from local village issues to global geopolitical shifts.

sections.heading: The Services at Stake
body: Successful candidates are allocated to various services based on their rank and preferences. These services are broadly classified into two categories:

1. All India Services: These services are common to both the Union and State governments. Officers are recruited by the Centre but their services are placed under various State cadres, and they are liable to serve both the Centre and the States.
2. Central Civil Services (Group 'A' and 'B'): These services function directly under the Government of India and are involved in the administration of Union subjects.

sections.heading: The Three-Tiered Selection Gauntlet
body: The CSE is a multi-layered process where each stage serves as a progressively finer filter to identify the most suitable candidates. The entire cycle, from notification to the final result, spans over a year.

Stage 1: Preliminary Examination (The Great Filter): This is an objective-type (Multiple Choice Questions) screening test. With an application pool often exceeding a million candidates for roughly 10,000-15,000 Mains spots, its primary role is elimination. It tests the breadth of a candidate's knowledge and their aptitude for logical reasoning. Crucially, the marks from this stage are not counted for the final merit list. It is a pass/fail gateway to the next level.

Stage 2: Main Examination (The Crucible of Knowledge): Candidates who clear the Prelims undertake the Main Examination, a descriptive (written) exam that is the real test of intellectual depth and analytical skill. Spread over nine papers, it evaluates a candidate's ability to articulate nuanced arguments, structure comprehensive answers, and demonstrate mastery over their chosen optional subject. The marks from the Main Examination are the most significant component of the final score.

Stage 3: Personality Test (The Final Appraisal): The final stage is an interview conducted by a board of distinguished experts at the UPSC headquarters in New Delhi. It is explicitly described as a "purposive conversation" rather than a strict cross-examination. The board, having access to the candidate's Detailed Application Form (DAF), assesses their personality, mental alertness, leadership qualities, and suitability for a high-stakes career in public administration.
The Final Verdict: Merit and Allocation

sections.heading: Typical Timeline (Indicative)
body: The UPSC Civil Services Examination is a marathon that unfolds over a period of 14-15 months, from the date of notification to the start of the Foundation Course. Understanding this timeline is crucial for strategic planning, sustained preparation, and mental conditioning. The following is a typical, indicative schedule.
Disclaimer: These timelines are based on past trends. Always refer to the official UPSC calendar for the specific year for exact dates.
Phase 1: Notification & Application (February - March)

Early February: The official notification for the Civil Services Examination is released by UPSC on its website (upsc.gov.in). This document is the bible for aspirants, containing all essential details: vacancy numbers, eligibility criteria, syllabus, exam rules, and the list of examination centers.

February - March: The online application window opens on the day of the notification and typically remains active for about 20-25 days . This process involves a one-time registration (OTR) and filling out the application form in two parts. Aspirants must be extremely careful while filling in details, selecting centers (which are allotted on a first-apply-first-allot basis), and uploading documents.
Phase 2: Prelims Preparation & Admit Card (April - May)
April - May: This is a period of intense, focused preparation and revision for the Preliminary Examination.

Late April / Early May: Approximately 3-4 weeks before the exam date , UPSC releases the e-Admit Card for the Preliminary Examination. Candidates must download and print it. It is mandatory to carry the admit card along with a valid, original Photo ID to the examination hall.
Phase 3: Preliminary Examination (Late May / Early June)

The Preliminary Exam is conducted on a single day (usually a Sunday). It consists of two compulsory papers with a break in between. Paper I: General Studies (9:30 AM to 11:30 AM) Paper II: CSAT (2:30 PM to 4:30 PM)
Paper I: General Studies (9:30 AM to 11:30 AM)
Paper II: CSAT (2:30 PM to 4:30 PM)
Phase 4: Mains Qualification & DAF-I (July - August)
Mid to Late July: The results of the Preliminary Examination are typically declared within 30-40 days of the exam date. UPSC releases a list of the roll numbers of qualified candidates.

July - August: Shortly after the Prelims result, the qualified candidates are required to fill out the Detailed Application Form-I (DAF-I) . This is an exhaustive form that collects detailed information about the candidate's personal background, educational qualifications, parental details, and employment history. It is also where candidates must indicate their optional subject for the Main Exam and provide preferences for services and cadres. This form is the basis for the interview later on.
Phase 5: Main Examination (September / October)
Late August / Early September: Admit cards for the Main Examination are released for candidates who have successfully submitted their DAF-I.

September / October: The Main Examination is a descriptive (written) test conducted over 5 days , usually spread across two weekends. It consists of 9 papers, testing the depth of a candidate's knowledge and analytical ability.
Phase 6: Personality Test Qualification & DAF-II (December - January)

December / Early January: The results of the Main Examination are usually announced about 2.5 to 3 months after the exam. A list of candidates who have qualified for the Personality Test (Interview) is published.

January: Qualified candidates are then required to fill the Detailed Application Form-II (DAF-II) . This form often requires them to reconfirm their service preferences and provide additional details which might be used by the interview board.
Phase 7: Personality Tests (Interviews) (February - April)
The Personality Tests (Interviews) typically commence a few weeks after the Mains results are declared.
Candidates are summoned to the UPSC office (Dholpur House) in New Delhi in batches. The interview schedule is spread over several weeks, often concluding by mid or late April.
Phase 8: Final Result Declaration (Late April / May)

This is the culmination of the entire process. The final merit list, based on the combined scores of the Main Examination and the Personality Test, is declared. This usually happens within 5-10 days of the conclusion of the last interview.
Phase 9: Post-Result Formalities (June - August)
The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) undertakes the crucial task of service and cadre allocation based on ranks, preferences, category, and vacancies.

Late August / Early September: The Foundation Course for all newly recruited officers begins at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) in Mussoorie, officially starting their journey as civil servants.

sections.heading: Eligibility Criteria
body: Before embarking on the rigorous journey of UPSC preparation, every aspirant must meticulously verify their eligibility. The criteria set by the Union Public Service Commission are strict and non-negotiable. Eligibility is primarily determined by four key parameters: Nationality, Age Limit, Educational Qualification, and Number of Attempts.
Note: The details provided here are based on prevailing rules. These are subject to change, and the official UPSC notification for the current examination year is the ultimate authority.
1. Nationality
The nationality requirement varies depending on the service an individual aspires to join.
For Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Foreign Service (IFS): The candidate must be a citizen of India . There are no exceptions for these premier services.
A citizen of India, or
A subject of Nepal, or

A Tibetan refugee who came over to India before the 1st of January, 1962, with the intention of permanently settling in India, or

A person of Indian origin (PIO) who has migrated from Pakistan, Burma, Sri Lanka, East African countries of Kenya, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi, Zaire, Ethiopia and Vietnam with the intention of permanently settling in India.
Candidates belonging to the latter categories must possess a certificate of eligibility issued by the Government of India.
2. Age Limit
The age of a candidate is calculated as of a specific cut-off date, which is typically the 1st of August of the examination year. The general age limits are as follows:
Minimum Age: A candidate must have attained the age of 21 years .
Maximum Age: A candidate must not have attained the age of 32 years (for the General category).
This means a candidate from the General category must have been born not earlier than 2nd August, 1993 and not later than 1st August, 2004 (for the 2025 exam, as an example).
UPSC provides relaxations in the upper age limit for candidates belonging to reserved categories:
Note: Cumulative relaxations are generally not allowed. For instance, an OBC candidate with a benchmark disability can claim a relaxation of 10 years, not 10 + 3 years.
3. Educational Qualification

sections.heading: The minimum educational requirement is straightforward
body: A candidate must hold a Bachelor's degree from any university incorporated by an Act of the Central or State Legislature in India or other educational institutions established by an Act of Parliament or declared to be deemed as a University under Section-3 of the UGC Act, 1956.
Alternatively, a candidate can possess an equivalent qualification.

Final-Year Students: Candidates who have appeared or intend to appear for their final degree examination and are awaiting results are also eligible to apply. However, they must produce proof of passing the said examination when they apply for the Main Examination.
Professional and technical qualifications recognized by the Government as equivalent to a professional and technical degree would also be sufficient.
4. Number of Attempts
The number of times a candidate can appear for the Preliminary Examination is limited. Appearing in even one paper of the Preliminary Exam is counted as an attempt.

An attempt is counted only if a candidate physically appears for at least one paper in the Preliminary Examination. Filling out the application form but not showing up for the exam does not count as an attempt.

sections.heading: Stages, Exam Pattern & Marking Scheme
body: The Civil Services Examination is a meticulously designed three-stage process. Each stage has a distinct purpose, format, and evaluation methodology. A thorough understanding of this pattern is the first step toward building a successful preparation strategy.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Preliminary Examination (Objective Type)
body: The primary purpose of the Prelims is to screen candidates for the Main Examination. It is a test of wide-ranging general knowledge and mental aptitude. The marks obtained in this stage are not counted for the final merit list.
Objective Format: Both papers consist of Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs).

Negative Marking: There is a penalty for incorrect answers. For each wrong answer, one-third (1/3rd) of the marks assigned to that question will be deducted. For a 2-mark question, this means a deduction of 0.66 marks.

CSAT is Qualifying: Paper II (CSAT) is a qualifying paper. A candidate must score a minimum of 33% (i.e., 66 out of 200 marks) in this paper. If a candidate fails to score 33% in CSAT, their Paper I (GS) will not be evaluated, and they will be disqualified.

Merit Calculation: The cut-off for qualifying for the Main Examination is determined solely based on the marks scored in General Studies Paper I , provided the candidate has scored the minimum qualifying marks in CSAT.

sections.heading: Stage 2: Main Examination (Descriptive Type)
body: This stage is the core of the selection process and is designed to assess the intellectual depth and understanding of a candidate rather than just their memory. The marks obtained here are the primary determinant of a candidate's final rank. It consists of 9 descriptive papers.
Candidates must clear these language papers to have their other Mains papers evaluated.
These papers are of matriculation or equivalent standard. Candidates from certain North-Eastern states may be exempted from Paper A.
The sum of marks from these seven papers determines the written score for the final merit list.
Candidates choose one optional subject from a list provided by UPSC, which has two papers.

sections.heading: Stage 3: Personality Test (Interview)
body: The final stage is a face-to-face interview with the UPSC board. It is not a test of knowledge, which has already been evaluated in the Mains, but an assessment of personality, suitability for public service, and mental calibre.
Maximum Marks: 275 Marks
Basis of Interview: The conversation is largely guided by the candidate's Detailed Application Form (DAF), covering their hobbies, academic background, work experience, and service preferences.

Qualities Assessed: The board evaluates mental alertness, critical powers of assimilation, clear and logical exposition, balance of judgment, variety and depth of interest, ability for social cohesion and leadership, and intellectual and moral integrity.
Final Rank Calculation
The final merit list is prepared based on the cumulative score of the Main Examination and the Personality Test.
Main Exam (Written) Marks: 1750 + Personality Test (Interview) Marks: 275 = Grand Total: 2025 Marks

Late January / Early February: Approximately 3 weeks before the exam date , UPSC releases the e-Admit Card for the Preliminary Examination. Candidates must download and print it.
Phase 3: Preliminary Examination (February)

The Preliminary Exam is conducted on a single day (usually a Sunday in February). It consists of two compulsory papers with a break in between. Paper I: General Studies & Engineering Aptitude (10:00 AM to 12:00 PM) Paper II: Engineering Discipline Specific (2:00 PM to 5:00 PM)
Paper I: General Studies & Engineering Aptitude (10:00 AM to 12:00 PM)
Paper II: Engineering Discipline Specific (2:00 PM to 5:00 PM)
Phase 4: Mains Qualification & DAF-I (April - May)
Late March / Early April: The results of the Preliminary Examination are typically declared within 30-40 days of the exam date. UPSC releases a list of the roll numbers of qualified candidates.

April - May: Shortly after the Prelims result, the qualified candidates are required to fill out the Detailed Application Form-I (DAF-I) . This is an exhaustive form that collects detailed information about the candidate's personal background, educational qualifications, and service preferences. This form is the basis for the interview later on.
Phase 5: Main Examination (June / July)
May / June: Admit cards for the Main Examination are released for candidates who have successfully submitted their DAF-I.

June / July: The Main Examination is a descriptive (written) test conducted on a single day, with two sessions for the two discipline-specific papers. It tests the depth of a candidate's technical knowledge and problem-solving ability.
Phase 6: Personality Test Qualification (September / October)

September / October: The results of the Main Examination are usually announced about 2 to 3 months after the exam. A list of candidates who have qualified for the Personality Test (Interview) is published.
Phase 7: Personality Tests (Interviews) (October - December)
The Personality Tests (Interviews) typically commence a few weeks after the Mains results are declared.
Candidates are summoned to the UPSC office (Dholpur House) in New Delhi in batches. The interview schedule is spread over several weeks.
Phase 8: Final Result Declaration (December / January)

This is the culmination of the entire process. The final merit list, based on the combined scores of the Main Examination and the Personality Test, is declared. This usually happens within 10-15 days of the conclusion of the last interview.

sections.heading: Eligibility Criteria
body: Before embarking on the rigorous journey of UPSC ESE preparation, every aspirant must meticulously verify their eligibility. The criteria set by the Union Public Service Commission are strict and non-negotiable. Eligibility is primarily determined by three key parameters: Nationality, Age Limit, and Educational Qualification.
Note: The details provided here are based on prevailing rules. These are subject to change, and the official UPSC notification for the current examination year is the ultimate authority.
1. Nationality
A candidate for the Engineering Services Examination must be one of the following:
A citizen of India, or
A subject of Nepal, or
A subject of Bhutan, or
A Tibetan refugee who came over to India before the 1st of January, 1962, with the intention of permanently settling in India, or

A person of Indian origin (PIO) who has migrated from Pakistan, Burma, Sri Lanka, East African countries of Kenya, Uganda, the United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Malawi, Zaire, Ethiopia and Vietnam with the intention of permanently settling in India.
Candidates belonging to the latter categories must possess a certificate of eligibility issued by the Government of India.
2. Age Limit
The age of a candidate is calculated as of a specific cut-off date, which is typically the 1st of January of the examination year. The general age limits are as follows:
Minimum Age: A candidate must have attained the age of 21 years .
Maximum Age: A candidate must not have attained the age of 30 years (for the General category).
This means a candidate from the General category must have been born not earlier than 2nd January, 1996 and not later than 1st January, 2005 (for the 2026 exam, as an example).
UPSC provides relaxations in the upper age limit for candidates belonging to reserved categories:
3. Educational Qualification
This is the most critical eligibility criterion for ESE. The minimum educational requirement is:

A candidate must have obtained an Engineering Degree from a University incorporated by an Act of the Central or State Legislature in India or other Educational Institutions established by an Act of Parliament or declared to be deemed as Universities under Section 3 of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956.
Alternatively, a candidate must have passed Sections A and B of the Institution Examinations of the Institution of Engineers (India).
Obtained a degree/diploma in Engineering from such foreign University/College/Institution and under such conditions as may be recognised by the Government for the purpose from time to time.
Passed Graduate Membership Examination of the Institution of Electronics and Telecommunication Engineers (India).
Passed Associate Membership Examination Parts II and III/Sections A and B of the Aeronautical Society of India.

Final-Year Students: Candidates who have appeared or intend to appear for their final degree examination and are awaiting results are also eligible to apply. However, they must produce proof of passing the said examination along with the Detailed Application Form (DAF-I) for the Main Examination.
The degree must be in one of the four eligible disciplines: Civil, Mechanical, Electrical, or Electronics & Telecommunication Engineering .
4. Number of Attempts

There is no restriction on the number of times a candidate can appear for the ESE. Candidates can attempt the examination as many times as they wish, provided they fulfill the age limit and other eligibility criteria specified in the examination notification.

sections.heading: Stages, Exam Pattern & Marking Scheme
body: The Engineering Services Examination is a meticulously designed three-stage process. Each stage has a distinct purpose, format, and evaluation methodology. A thorough understanding of this pattern is the first step toward building a successful preparation strategy.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Preliminary Examination (Objective Type)
body: The primary purpose of the Prelims is to screen candidates for the Main Examination. It tests both general aptitude and core engineering knowledge. The marks obtained in this stage are not counted for the final merit list.
Objective Format: Both papers consist of Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs).
Negative Marking: There is a penalty for incorrect answers. For each wrong answer, one-third (1/3rd) of the marks assigned to that question will be deducted.

Cut-off Calculation: The cut-off for qualifying for the Main Examination is determined based on the total marks scored in both Paper I and Paper II. There are minimum qualifying marks for each paper as decided by the commission.

sections.heading: Stage 2: Main Examination (Descriptive Type)
body: This stage is the core of the selection process and is designed to assess the in-depth technical knowledge and problem-solving skills of a candidate. The marks obtained here are the primary determinant of a candidate's final rank. It consists of 2 descriptive papers specific to the candidate's engineering stream.
Both papers are subjective and require detailed, written answers. The use of non-programmable scientific calculators is permitted in this stage.

sections.heading: Stage 3: Personality Test (Interview)
body: The final stage is a face-to-face interview with the UPSC board. It is not just a test of technical knowledge but an assessment of the candidate's overall personality, leadership potential, and suitability for a high-responsibility technical career in the government.
Maximum Marks: 200 Marks
Basis of Interview: The conversation is largely guided by the candidate's Detailed Application Form (DAF), covering their academic and project background, work experience, and interests.
Qualities Assessed: The board evaluates leadership, initiative, intellectual curiosity, judgement, mental alertness, and the ability to apply technical knowledge to practical situations.
Final Rank Calculation
The final merit list is prepared based on the cumulative score of the Main Examination and the Personality Test.
Main Exam (Written) Marks: 600 + Personality Test (Interview) Marks: 200 = Grand Total: 800 Marks
Application Workflow

The application process for the UPSC ESE is conducted exclusively online through the official UPSC website. It is a meticulous process that requires careful attention to detail. Any error can lead to the rejection of the application. The process can be broken down into several key stages.

sections.heading: Stage 1: One-Time Registration (OTR)
body: Before filling out the application form for any UPSC examination, a candidate must complete the One-Time Registration. As the name suggests, this is a one-time activity.

Purpose: The OTR platform saves a candidate's basic personal information, which can then be automatically populated whenever they apply for a UPSC exam. This saves time and reduces the chance of errors in subsequent applications.

Information Required: You will need to provide your name, parents' names, date of birth, gender, minority status, a valid mobile number, a valid email ID, and details of your Class 10 board examination roll number.

Verification: The mobile number and email ID are verified through OTPs. It is crucial to use an active and personal mobile number and email, as all future communication from UPSC will be sent to them.
Permanence: The information submitted in the OTR profile is stored securely and can be updated, with some limitations, at any time.

sections.heading: Stage 2: Filling the Examination Application Form
body: Once your OTR is complete, you can log in and apply for the Engineering Services (Preliminary) Examination. This is typically a two-part process.
